newsitem.title: TURKEY: FOCUS-Political woes depress Turkey's markets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Political woes depress Turkey's markets.

text.p: Turkey's central bank moved on Tuesday to limit the financial fallout from the country's political crisis, while declines in stock prices gathered pace ahead of an expected handover of political power.

Market participants said the central bank allowed overnight money and repo rates to soar, aiming to curb the rising demand for dollars that accompanies Turkey's frequent bouts of political uncertainty.

They said the central bank did not provide its usual funding to state banks for heavy mid-month public sector salary payments late on Monday, causing the market to fall extremely short and sending ripples through the rest of the financial sector.
"The central bank is acting to control the foreign currency rates by further tightening the liquidity," said one banker.

Driving the bank's moves was nervousness before a June 18 deadline, imposed by the coalition's secularist wing, for Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan to step down and make way for a conservative caretaker to lead Turkey to fresh polls.
Erbakan is locked in a battle with the secularist establishment, including the military, over what it says is a rise in Moslem activism. The planned power swap is designed to ease that pressure.
On Tuesday, Erbakan said his battered coalition -- now stripped of a majority in parliament -- could muster the MPs needed to manage the transfer of power and set new polls.
The money market opened 34.6 trillion lira ($238 million) short on Tuesday. The average overnight repo rate jumped to 84.42 percent from Monday's 78.61.
Money market moves dragged shares lower, brokers said.
"Rising overnight (repo and money) rates negatively affected the (stock) market, too. I do not expect political uncertainty to fade much tomorrow," said Ali Guler from Acar Securities.
The Istanbul Stock Exchange Index ended the day down 1.96 percent at 1,551, with volume rising 6.8 percent from a day earlier to 12.9 trillion lira ($89 million).
"The market is gripped by uncertainty due to the expected resignation of the government. The index has support at the 1,550 level and the next support is seen at 1,530," he added.

"It looks as though the central bank began acting on its own (to control the markets), independently from the government. This further raised suspicions that the coalition would not last," said one private banker.
"But the central bank's move is correct although belated," he said.
The prevailing mood also undermined the Treasury's auction of two-year, inflation-indexed bonds.

Officials said the Treasury managed to sell just 3.05 trillion lira ($20.9 million) worth of paper, down sharply from 198.1 trillion ($1.36 billion) worth of similar, three-month coupon payment bonds sold on June 3. Both auctions saw a risk premium of 32 percent.
Bankers have long been complaining that trade in these bonds was very weak because of the funding risks involved in buying such long-term paper amid political concerns.
But the Treasury has insisted on issuing these instruments in the last six auctions held since the beginning of April.

"In an environment where the future of the government is unknown, an alteration in the prime ministry is imminent and funding costs have jumped to almost 90 percent levels, there is no logic in buying paper," said another private banker.
The lira weakened to 145,720 against the dollar from a close of 145,400 on Monday. Bond yields rose to 111.5 percent from 108.5 percent. ($1=145,720 lira)
